units.title: Sacraments: encounters with Christ
units.eq: How does Jesus meet us today?

lessons.title: Christ in the sacraments
lessons.idea: In the sacraments Jesus himself acts. Each is an outward sign that gives the grace it signifies, like the touch that healed the paralyzed man in Luke 5. The Church is the sacrament of Christ’s presence in the world.
lessons.question: What is a sign? What does it do?
lessons.activity: “Matter and form” lab (30 min). For Baptism (water; “I baptize you…”), Eucharist (bread and wine; words of consecration), Anointing (oil; the prayer), children match matter, form and minister on cards. Then explain why both are needed: the sign and the word.
teach: “What was visible in our Savior has passed over into his mysteries” (St Leo; CCC 1115). Jesus healed by touch, and now acts through the sacraments (CCC 1116).
A sacrament is an efficacious sign: it brings about what it signifies (CCC 1084, 1127). It has matter (the thing), form (the words) and a minister (CCC 1131).
The sacraments work by Christ’s own power, not the minister’s holiness (CCC 1128), but they bear fruit according to the faith of the receiver (CCC 1128).
Say plainly that grace is God’s life in us, a gift we cannot earn (CCC 1996–1999).
talk: What is the difference between a sign and a sacrament?
Which sacrament uses oil? Which uses bread and wine?
How do the sacraments help in daily life?
quiz: A sacrament…|Is a sign that gives grace|Is a ritual to impress|Is a school|Is only a symbol|0|CCC 1131.
“Matter and form” refer to…|The date and time|The sign and the words|The priest and server|The church and altar|1|CCC 1084.
Who instituted the sacraments?|The Pope|The apostles alone|The saints|Christ|3|CCC 1114.
lessons.life: Look for the matter of a sacrament in your parish (water, oil, bread, wine) and learn its words.
lessons.saint: Thomas Aquinas: wrote the hymn Pange Lingua for Corpus Christi.
misc: “I get grace by just being present.”
lessons.mem: “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” (Matthew 9:2)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 5:17–26 up to the roof being opened. Ask, “What would you do for a friend?” Then finish the story and ask what Jesus did: he spoke and touched. He still does.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain for one sacrament its matter, form and minister.

lessons.title: Three groups of sacraments
lessons.idea: The seven sacraments fall into three groups that match three needs of life: initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist) gives life, healing (Reconciliation, Anointing) restores it, and service of communion (Holy Orders, Matrimony) builds the Church.
lessons.question: How does each group serve people?
lessons.activity: “Life map” flowchart (25 min). Students draw a life path (birth, growing, falling ill, falling into sin, committing to a vocation) and mark which sacrament meets each moment. Add the signs. Read Acts 2:38 to see how early Christians began.
teach: Sacraments of Christian initiation lay the foundations of life (CCC 1212). Penance and Anointing heal (CCC 1421). Holy Orders and Matrimony are ordered to others’ salvation (CCC 1534).
The three groups echo human life: birth, growth, nourishment, healing, mission. Christian life is a real life in Christ.
Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders can only be received once because they imprint a character (CCC 1121). The others can be repeated.
Point out that Matrimony and Orders are not “better” or “worse”: both serve the community.
talk: What human need does each group meet?
Which do you look forward to?
quiz: Penance is a sacrament of…|Healing|Marriage|Service|Initiation|0|CCC 1421.
Holy Orders is a sacrament of…|Service|Healing|Birth|Initiation|0|CCC 1534.
Baptism is a sacrament of…|Healing|Initiation|Service|Vocation|1|CCC 1212.
lessons.life: Ask a parent which sacraments they received and when.
lessons.saint: Francis de Sales: spiritual guide for ordinary people.
misc: “You can repeat Baptism if you fall away.”
lessons.mem: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins.” (Acts 2:38)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What do people need to be born, to get well, to belong?” Write the answers, then map them to the sacraments.
lessons.assess: Give a life situation and ask students to name the group and the sacrament.

lessons.title: Signs and symbols
lessons.idea: The Church’s liturgy uses signs and symbols: water, oil, light, bread, wine, incense, gestures. They come from creation and the Bible, and are filled with new meaning by Christ.
lessons.question: What do these signs mean?
lessons.activity: “Symbol museum” (30 min). Display real objects and let students explain them to a partner: water (washing and new life), oil (strength and anointing), light (Christ), incense (prayer rising), bread/wine (Eucharist), hands (blessing), kneeling (adoration). Match each to a verse (Psalm 51:7; Psalm 141:2; John 8:12).
teach: In the liturgy, signs from creation, human life and the covenant are assumed by Christ (CCC 1145–1152). Water, oil, bread and wine each have deep biblical roots.
Gestures and postures speak: standing for respect and joy, kneeling for adoration, bowing for reverence, the Sign of the Cross for faith (CCC 1155–1162).
Images (icons, statues) honor persons, not material things (CCC 1159–1162). Sacred music and art lift our minds to God.
Teach that symbols are not decorations. Ask what each shows about God.
quiz: Oil signifies…|Cleaning|Cooking only|Rest|Strength and the Spirit|3|CCC 1293.
Light signifies…|Fire only|Christ|Noise|Electricity|1|CCC 1189.
The laying on of hands signifies…|Waving|Giving the Spirit|Fear|Greeting|1|CCC 1150.
lessons.life: Notice and name three signs at Mass this Sunday.
lessons.saint: Pope St John Paul II: taught about the signs of the liturgy.
misc: “Incense and candles are just for show.”
lessons.mem: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you.” (Psalm 141:2)
lessons.hook: Show a flag, a wedding ring, a handshake. “What do these say without words?” Then reveal a candle, a cup of water, a bottle of oil.
lessons.assess: Ask students to choose a symbol and explain what it means and where it appears in church.

lessons.title: Baptism
lessons.idea: Baptism is the gateway to the other sacraments. It forgives original sin and all personal sin, makes us children of God, and joins us to the Church. Its sign is water poured three times with the words “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
lessons.question: What are the effects of Baptism?
lessons.activity: “Baptism step by step” (30 min). Lay out the rite on cards: sign of the cross, readings, anointing with the oil of catechumens, blessing of water, renunciation and profession of faith, pouring, chrism, white garment, candle. Students put them in order and say what each means. Read Romans 6:3–4.
teach: Baptism is “the basis of the whole Christian life, the gateway to life in the Spirit” (CCC 1213). It removes original and personal sin and brings new birth (CCC 1263–1264).
Romans 6:3–4: we are buried with Christ and raised to new life. The water has been a sign of death and life since the Flood and the Red Sea (CCC 1217–1222).
Ordinarily a bishop, priest or deacon baptizes, but in an emergency anyone can, with water and the words (CCC 1256). Infants are baptized because grace is a gift (CCC 1250–1252).
Baptism marks the soul forever (CCC 1272–1274). Adults who are not baptized prepare through the catechumenate (RCIA).
talk: What does the white garment signify?
What do you renounce at Baptism?
quiz: Baptism removes…|Original sin and personal sin|Shyness|Hunger|Nothing|0|CCC 1263.
Baptism imprints…|An indelible character|A bruise|A name only|A tattoo|0|CCC 1272.
The ordinary minister is…|A bishop, priest or deacon|Anyone|A teacher|A parent only|0|CCC 1256.
lessons.life: Renew your baptismal promises at Easter.
misc: “Unbaptized babies cannot be saved” (the Church entrusts them to God’s mercy, CCC 1261).
lessons.mem: “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5)
lessons.hook: Pour water into a bowl and ask, “What does water do?” (cleans, quenches, gives life, can drown). Say the Church uses all four meanings in Baptism.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the effects of Baptism and the roles of matter, form and minister.

lessons.title: Confirmation
lessons.idea: Confirmation completes Baptism. The bishop (or a priest delegated) anoints the forehead with chrism and says “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit.” We receive the seven gifts and are sent to witness.
lessons.question: What gifts do we receive?
lessons.activity: “Seven gifts” chart (25 min). Students make a card for each gift (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord / wonder and awe), write a definition, and give an example for each. Read Acts 8:14–17. Then plan the next parish Confirmation prayer.
teach: Confirmation perfects baptismal grace and seals us with the Spirit (CCC 1285, 1302–1303). The sign is anointing with chrism by the laying on of hands and the words “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1300).
The seven gifts of the Spirit (Isaiah 11:2) strengthen us for witness (CCC 1830–1831). The fruits (love, joy, peace…) show them at work (CCC 1832).
The ordinary minister is the bishop, which shows our bond with the apostles; priests may confirm in some cases (CCC 1312–1313).
Confirmation is a beginning, not a graduation. Invite students to name how they will witness.
talk: How have you seen the fruits in someone?
quiz: The matter of Confirmation is…|Water|Ashes|Chrism|Bread|2|CCC 1297.
Confirmation seals us with…|A name|A medal|The Holy Spirit|A ring|2|CCC 1302.
One of the fruits of the Spirit is…|Wealth|Joy|Fame|Speed|1|Galatians 5:22.
lessons.life: Pray the Veni Sancte Spiritus or Come Holy Spirit daily.
misc: “Confirmation means I confirm my faith, and it’s optional.”
“Confirmation is the end of religious ed.”
lessons.mem: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love.
lessons.hook: Ask, “What was different about the apostles before and after Pentecost?” (hiding versus preaching). Confirmation gives the same Spirit for the same mission.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name all seven gifts and tell the sign and words of Confirmation.

lessons.title: Living as the baptized
lessons.idea: By Baptism we share in Christ’s three roles: priest (offering our lives to God), prophet (witnessing to the truth) and king (serving others). Every baptized person has a mission.
lessons.question: How do you live your baptism?
lessons.activity: “Baptismal promise card” (25 min). Students write a personal card with three promises: one as priest (pray/offer a sacrifice this week), one as prophet (speak up for truth or a friend), one as king (serve someone). Read 1 Peter 2:9.
teach: Through Baptism we share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly office (CCC 897–913, 783–786). The ordained priesthood and the common priesthood differ in kind, not only in degree (CCC 1547).
Priest: offer our work, prayers, joys and sufferings with Christ (CCC 901, 1141). Prophet: witness to the faith in word and life (CCC 904–907). King: master ourselves and serve (CCC 908–913).
“You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). The laity bring Christ into the world (CCC 898–900).
Link to the baptismal promises renewed at Easter.
talk: How do you serve as a priest, prophet and king?
quiz: The baptized share in Christ as…|Judge, jury, executioner|Priest, prophet and king|Teacher, lawyer, doctor|Soldier, farmer, merchant|1|CCC 897.
To be a prophet is to…|Hide|Witness to Christ|Predict lottery numbers|Lead armies|1|CCC 904.
Kingship means…|Buying|Hiding|Ruling harshly|Serving|3|CCC 908.
lessons.life: Do a small act of service in your parish.
lessons.mem: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation.” (1 Peter 2:9)
lessons.hook: Show a crown, a scroll and a chalice. “Who has all three?” (Jesus). Then say: we share in all three.
lessons.assess: Ask each student to give one example of acting as priest, prophet and king.

lessons.title: The source and summit
lessons.idea: The Eucharist is “the source and summit of the Christian life.” Every sacrament and work of the Church flows from it and leads to it, because in it we have Christ himself.
lessons.question: Why “source and summit”?
lessons.activity: “Source and summit” diagram (25 min). In a circle put the Eucharist, then draw arrows from and to it for each sacrament, the parish ministries, prayer, service. Read John 6:35 and discuss: “I am the bread of life.”
teach: “The Eucharist is the source and summit of the Christian life” (Lumen Gentium 11; CCC 1324). The other sacraments and ministries are bound up with it (CCC 1325).
It is called by many names: Thanksgiving, Lord’s Supper, Breaking of Bread, Holy Sacrifice, Holy Communion (CCC 1328–1332).
At the Last Supper Jesus instituted it “on the night he was betrayed” and commanded “Do this in memory of me” (Luke 22:19; CCC 1337–1340).
Use John 6:35 (“I am the bread of life”) to connect Scripture to the sacrament.
talk: Why is the Eucharist the center?
What other names do we use?
quiz: The Eucharist is the…|Surprise|Beginning only|Source and summit|Option|2|CCC 1324.
“Eucharist” means…|Thanksgiving|Party|Meal|Sacrifice|0|CCC 1328.
Another name is…|Game|Prayer|Holy Communion|Show|2|CCC 1331.
lessons.life: Offer a prayer of thanks after Communion.
lessons.saint: Pier Giorgio Frassati: he loved the Eucharist.
lessons.mem: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger.” (John 6:35)
lessons.hook: Draw a mountain with a stream starting near the top. “Where does the stream begin and where does it end?” The Eucharist is both the source and the goal.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “source and summit” in their own words.

lessons.title: The Real Presence
lessons.idea: In the Eucharist, bread and wine become the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of Jesus Christ. The Church calls this transubstantiation. Christ is really, truly and substantially present.
lessons.question: How do we know Jesus is truly present?
lessons.activity: “Witness file” (30 min). Teams review the evidence: Scripture (John 6; Luke 22:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–29), the Fathers (Ignatius of Antioch, Justin Martyr, Cyril of Jerusalem) and the Church’s teaching (CCC 1373–1381). Each writes a one-paragraph “case.” Then gather around a tabernacle for a silent visit.
teach: Christ is present in the Church gathered, in the Word, in the priest and, above all, “in the Eucharistic species” (CCC 1373). This is real presence “in the fullest sense” (CCC 1374).
Transubstantiation: the substance of bread and wine become Christ’s Body and Blood, while the appearances remain (CCC 1376–1377). Trent (1551) defined this (CCC 1376).
Early Christians believed this. St Ignatius (c. 107) calls the Eucharist “the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ” (CCC 1374). Justin Martyr (c. 155) says the same.
Eucharistic adoration flows from this belief (CCC 1378–1381). Teach reverent behavior before the tabernacle.
quiz: Transubstantiation means…|Nothing changes|Bread symbolizes Christ|Christ is only remembered|The substance of bread and wine becomes Christ’s Body and Blood|3|CCC 1376.
The Real Presence includes…|Only memory|Body, blood, soul and divinity|Only the Body|Only a feeling|1|CCC 1374.
We kneel to…|Adore|Hide|Pray silently|Rest|0|CCC 1378.
lessons.life: Spend 10 minutes with Jesus in the tabernacle.
misc: “It changes only when we believe it.”
lessons.mem: “This is my body, which is given for you.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Read John 6:51–58 slowly. Ask what Jesus says (“my flesh is true food”) and what the crowd did (many left). “He did not say, ‘I was only speaking in symbols.’ ”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what happens at consecration, using “substance” and “appearance.”

lessons.title: Receiving Communion
lessons.idea: To receive Communion worthily we believe the Church’s faith, are in the state of grace (free of mortal sin), fast for one hour, and come with reverence. Afterward we give thanks.
lessons.question: How do we prepare?
lessons.activity: “Before and after” prayer cards (25 min). Students write a preparation prayer and a thanksgiving prayer. Practice reverent reception: stepping up, bowing, “Amen,” hands (on tongue or in hands), and moving away. Look at the Anima Christi.
teach: To receive, one must be in the state of grace (CCC 1385). Anyone aware of mortal sin should go to Confession first (CCC 1415; 1 Corinthians 11:27–29).
One hour fast from food and drink (water and medicine excepted) shows respect (Canon 919; CCC 1387). Reverent gestures express faith.
Fruits of Communion: union with Christ, forgiveness of venial sin, preservation from mortal sin, unity of the Church, commitment to the poor (CCC 1391–1397).
Non-Catholics are warmly invited to a blessing or to pray, since reception expresses full communion (CCC 1398–1401).
quiz: The Eucharistic fast is…|Ten minutes|One week|One hour|One day|2|Canon 919.
To receive, one must be…|In a state of grace|A priest|Famous|An adult|0|CCC 1385.
When receiving, we say…|Please|Thanks|Amen|Hello|2|CCC 1389.
lessons.life: Write a prayer to say after Communion.
lessons.saint: Imelda Lambertini: patron of first communicants.
misc: “If I make a mistake, God will reject me.”
lessons.mem: Soul of Christ, sanctify me; Body of Christ, save me; Blood of Christ, inebriate me. (Anima Christi)
lessons.hook: Ask, “How would you prepare to meet a king?” Then, “Whom do we meet in Communion?” Read 1 Corinthians 11:27–29.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list the four ways to prepare and explain why we say “Amen.”

lessons.title: The Introductory Rites and Liturgy of the Word
lessons.idea: The Mass begins with the Introductory Rites, where we gather and repent, and the Liturgy of the Word, where God speaks. We hear the first reading, the psalm, the second reading, the Gospel, the homily, then pray the Creed and the Prayer of the Faithful.
lessons.question: What are the readings?
lessons.activity: “Follow the readings” (30 min). Distribute a Sunday missal or a printout of the readings. Students mark first reading, psalm, second reading, Alleluia, Gospel. Practice a response aloud. Then write a one-sentence summary of the Gospel and what it asks.
teach: Gather: entrance song, greeting, Penitential Act, Gloria, Collect (CCC 1348). We stand, sing and prepare our hearts.

Liturgy of the Word: first reading (usually the Old Testament), responsorial psalm, second reading (the letters), Alleluia and Gospel, homily, Creed, Prayer of the Faithful (CCC 1349). At the Gospel we stand because Christ himself speaks.
On Sundays the readings follow a three-year cycle (A, B, C) so that much of the Bible is read over time (CCC 1154).
God’s Word is truly proclaimed, not just read. Encourage students to listen for one line.
quiz: The first reading is usually from…|The Gospels|A letter|A book|The Old Testament|3|CCC 1349.
The homily explains…|The weather|The news|Sports|The readings|3|CCC 1349.
The Gospel is proclaimed by…|A priest or deacon|A child only|Anyone|A choir|0|CCC 1349.
lessons.life: Read next Sunday’s readings beforehand.
misc: “The Prayer of the Faithful is just announcements.”
lessons.mem: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” (Psalm 119:105)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What did you hear at Mass last Sunday?” Read Nehemiah 8:1–12, where the people stood, listened and wept for joy at the reading of the Law.
lessons.assess: Ask students to put the parts of the first half of Mass in order.

lessons.title: The Liturgy of the Eucharist
lessons.idea: In the Liturgy of the Eucharist the gifts of bread and wine are prepared, the Eucharistic Prayer is offered, and we receive Holy Communion. The central moment is the consecration.
lessons.question: What happens at the Consecration?
lessons.activity: “Order the steps” relay (25 min). Cards with: Preparation of the gifts, Preface, Sanctus, Epiclesis, Institution narrative, Memorial acclamation, Great Amen, Our Father, Sign of peace, Lamb of God, Communion, Prayer after Communion. Teams put them in order, then explain each one.
teach: Preparation of the gifts: bread and wine are brought forward and offered (CCC 1350). The priest prays that the sacrifice “may be acceptable to God the almighty Father.”

The Eucharistic Prayer is the heart: thanksgiving (Preface), Sanctus, epiclesis (asking the Spirit), institution narrative (the words of Christ), anamnesis (remembering), offering and intercessions (CCC 1352–1354).
Communion Rite: Our Father, sign of peace, breaking of bread (Lamb of God), Communion (CCC 1355). The priest acts “in persona Christi” (CCC 1548).
The Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary in an unbloody manner (CCC 1366–1367).
quiz: The Sanctus is…|Holy, Holy, Holy|Lamb of God|Creed|Our Father|0|CCC 1352.
The institution narrative recounts…|The Last Supper|Pentecost|Creation|Baptism|0|CCC 1353.
The Great Amen follows…|The Gospel|The creed|The homily|The doxology|3|CCC 1353.
lessons.life: Sing the Sanctus with attention.
lessons.saint: Isaiah: vision of Holy, holy, holy.
misc: “The Mass is a new sacrifice each time.”
lessons.mem: “Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Set a table and bring bread and wine. “What happens at Mass at this table?” Show Luke 22:19.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain epiclesis, institution narrative and communion in their own words.

lessons.title: Concluding Rites and mission
lessons.idea: The Concluding Rites bless us and send us out. “Ite, missa est” (“Go, you are sent”) gives the Mass its name. What we receive at Mass we are meant to give away.
lessons.question: What does “Ite, missa est” mean?
lessons.activity: “Sent!” service project (30 min). The class chooses a service project (card writing for the homebound, collecting food, cleaning up the church). Plan jobs, roles and a prayer. Close the planning with the dismissal and blessing.
teach: After Communion come the prayer, announcements, blessing and dismissal (CCC 1332, 1351). The words “Go in peace” or “Go and announce the Gospel of the Lord” send us out.
The Eucharist commits us to the poor (CCC 1397). We cannot receive Christ and ignore him in others (Matthew 25:40).
The Church’s precepts include attending Mass on Sundays and holy days and supporting the Church’s needs (CCC 2041–2043).
Encourage students to think of leaving Mass as the start of an assignment.
quiz: “Mass” comes from…|Message|Mass media|Messiah|Ite, missa est|3|CCC 1332.
The Mass ends with…|A sermon|The Gloria|A blessing and dismissal|Communion|2|CCC 1332.
We are sent to…|Hide|Rest|Wait|Love and serve|3|John 20:21.
lessons.life: After Mass, do one kind thing.
lessons.saint: Teresa of Calcutta: Eucharist leads to service.
lessons.mem: “Go into all the world and proclaim the Gospel to the whole creation.” (Mark 16:15)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What’s the difference between a meeting that ends and a mission that starts?” Read Mark 16:15 and ask who is being sent.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “Ite, missa est” and name one way they will live out Mass this week.

lessons.title: Sin and conversion
lessons.idea: Sin is an offense against God, reason and truth, and it wounds us and others. God calls everyone to conversion, a turning of the heart. Zacchaeus shows what real change looks like.
lessons.question: What is conversion?
lessons.activity: “Zacchaeus in action” (25 min). Act the scene in four frames: the tree, the call, the dinner, the promise. Then write a “return and repair” plan for a modern situation: if I took, I give back; if I hurt, I apologize. Pray the Act of Contrition.
teach: Conversion (metanoia) is a turning to God and away from sin (CCC 1427–1433). It is a gift of grace and demands our response.
Sin is “an offense against reason, truth and right conscience” (CCC 1849). It wounds our nature and harms solidarity (CCC 1849–1853).
Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and repays four times what he stole (Luke 19:8). Real contrition includes making amends.
Stress God’s initiative: Jesus says, “I must stay at your house today.” The Father runs to the prodigal (Luke 15).
quiz: Conversion is…|Changing clothes|Moving house|Winning|Turning toward God|3|CCC 1428.
Zacchaeus promised to…|Complain|Run|Repay and give to the poor|Hide|2|Luke 19:8.
Jesus said, “Today…”|You are late|Salvation has come|Go away|Sit|1|Luke 19:9.
lessons.life: Make a restitution this week if you owe someone.
lessons.saint: Matthew: tax collector who followed Christ.
lessons.mem: “Today salvation has come to this house.” (Luke 19:9)
lessons.hook: Ask, “What do you do when you take the wrong turn?” (Turn around.) Read Luke 19:1–10 and ask how Zacchaeus turned around.
lessons.assess: Ask students to retell the Zacchaeus story and name what conversion required.

lessons.title: The sacrament of Penance
lessons.idea: The Sacrament of Penance (Reconciliation) has four parts: contrition, confession, satisfaction (penance) and absolution. The priest acts in the person of Christ and is bound to total secrecy.
lessons.question: What are the four parts?
lessons.activity: “Confession walkthrough” (30 min). Mark out a room with stations: examination, contrition (Act of Contrition), confession, penance, absolution, thanksgiving. A volunteer adult plays priest and a student plays penitent with a fictional sin. Debrief on how it felt.
teach: Acts of the penitent: contrition, confession, satisfaction (CCC 1450–1460). Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect from fear or shame (CCC 1451–1453).
Absolution: “I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father…” (CCC 1449). The priest is bound by the sacramental seal, absolutely (CCC 1467).
We must confess all mortal sins, in kind and number; confessing venial sins is recommended (CCC 1456–1458). Receive the sacrament at least once a year (CCC 2042).
Prepare a simple examination for children. Normalize fear and show the joy of forgiveness.
quiz: The four parts: contrition, confession, penance and…|Absolution|Commandment|Conversation|Communion|0|CCC 1450-1460.
The words of absolution include…|I forget you|I absolve you|I judge you|I teach you|1|CCC 1449.
The seal of confession is…|Optional|Absolute|Broken|Shared|1|CCC 1467.
lessons.life: Plan to go to Confession during Advent or Lent.
misc: “The priest can tell others what I said.”
“If I forget a sin, the confession is invalid.”
lessons.mem: “I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” (Rite of Penance)
lessons.hook: Ask, “Who do you tell when you’ve done something wrong?” Recall John 20:21–23: Jesus gives apostles the power to forgive.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the four parts and the seal of confession.

lessons.title: Anointing of the Sick
lessons.idea: In the Anointing of the Sick, a priest anoints the forehead and hands with oil of the sick and prays, giving strength, peace and courage in serious illness or old age. It may also give physical healing if God wills.
lessons.question: When is it celebrated?
lessons.activity: “Visit and pray” (25 min). Students write cards for the sick and practice words of comfort. Role-play a priest’s visit with oil of the sick. Learn the prayers: “Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit.”
teach: James 5:14–15 describes the practice: elders anoint with oil and pray, and the Lord raises up and forgives (CCC 1499–1513).
The sacrament is for those who are seriously ill or weakened by age, and it can be repeated if the illness worsens (CCC 1514–1515). It is not only for the dying.
Its effects: strength, peace, forgiveness of sins, union with Christ’s Passion, sometimes bodily healing (CCC 1520–1523). The Viaticum (Communion for the dying) completes it (CCC 1524–1525).
Speak sensitively. Some students have ill relatives. Offer hope.
talk: How can you comfort the sick?
quiz: Anointing uses…|Water|Salt|Bread|Oil of the sick|3|CCC 1513.
It may be received…|More than once|By priests only|Never|Once only|0|CCC 1515.
It is celebrated for…|Serious illness or old age|Games|Colds|Exams|0|CCC 1514.
lessons.life: Visit or write to someone who is sick.
misc: “Last rites mean you’re about to die.”
“If the person isn’t healed, the sacrament failed.”
lessons.mem: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church.” (James 5:14)
lessons.hook: Ask who has been in the hospital or visited someone. “How do you show care?” Read James 5:14–15.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain who may receive the sacrament and its effects.

units.title: Holy Orders and Matrimony
units.eq: How do the sacraments serve others?

lessons.title: Holy Orders
lessons.idea: In Holy Orders Christ continues his priesthood through bishops, priests and deacons. Ordination marks the soul and configures the man to Christ the head and shepherd.
lessons.question: Who can be ordained?
lessons.activity: “Ministry interview” (30 min). Invite a priest or deacon (or watch a short interview) and let students ask prepared questions about his call and daily life. Draw the three degrees of Orders with their roles.
teach: Holy Orders has three degrees: bishop, priest, deacon (CCC 1554, 1536). Bishops are successors of the apostles. Priests are co-workers of bishops. Deacons serve in word, liturgy and charity (CCC 1555–1571).
Ordination imprints an indelible character and makes the priest act in persona Christi capitis (CCC 1548, 1581–1584). Jesus chose the Twelve (Luke 6:12–16) and the Church ordains only men (CCC 1577).
The minister of ordination is a bishop through the laying on of hands and the prayer of consecration (CCC 1572–1574).
Celibacy in the Latin Church is a discipline, not a doctrine; Eastern Churches ordain married men (CCC 1579–1580).
quiz: Holy Orders has…|One degree|Two degrees|Three degrees|Five degrees|2|CCC 1554.
The ordinary minister of ordination is…|A priest|A bishop|A layperson|A deacon|1|CCC 1576.
Priests act…|As kings|In the person of Christ|As teachers only|On their own|1|CCC 1548.
lessons.life: Pray for priests every day.
lessons.mem: “Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Ask, “Who leads a team, serves at a table and shepherds a flock?” Each image fits a role: bishop, deacon, priest.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the three degrees and one duty of each.

lessons.title: Matrimony
lessons.idea: In Matrimony a baptized man and woman make a covenant for life, ordered to their good and to children. It is a sacrament and a sign of Christ’s love for the Church.
lessons.question: What are the goods of marriage?
lessons.activity: “Wedding rite” (25 min). Walk through the rite: the entrance, readings, exchange of consent, rings, nuptial blessing. Students underline the vows. Compare with Jesus’ words in Matthew 19:4–6.
teach: Marriage was created by God and raised by Christ to a sacrament (CCC 1601–1617). The couple are the ministers; the priest or deacon witnesses (CCC 1623).
Four goods: unity, fidelity, indissolubility, openness to children (CCC 1643–1654). “What God has joined together, let no one put asunder” (Mark 10:9).
Marriage is a sign of Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5:25–32; CCC 1616). The family is “the domestic church” (CCC 1655–1658).
Be mindful of students whose families have experienced divorce. Speak with compassion and avoid blame.
talk: What are the goods of marriage?
quiz: The ministers of marriage are…|The parents|The priest|The witnesses|The couple|3|CCC 1623.
Marriage is…|Legal only|Temporary|Optional|Permanent|3|CCC 1640.
The family is…|A team|A club|The domestic church|A business|2|CCC 1655.
lessons.life: Thank a married couple you know.
lessons.saint: Zélie and Louis Martin: parents of Thérèse, canonized together as a married couple.
misc: “A married couple can cancel a sacramental marriage.”
lessons.mem: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.” (Mark 10:9)
lessons.hook: Show wedding photos or a ring. Read Genesis 2:18–24 and ask, “What did God see that was not good?” (being alone).
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four goods and the ministers of the sacrament.

lessons.title: Vocation
lessons.idea: Everyone has a vocation: first the call to holiness and then a particular way to live it, as a married person, a priest or deacon, a consecrated religious, or a dedicated single. We discern through prayer, Scripture, sacraments and wise guidance.
lessons.question: What is your call?
lessons.activity: “Listening for the call” (25 min). Students write a vocation prayer, “Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.” They list gifts they have, needs they see, and someone who could help them discern. Pray it silently for two minutes.
teach: All are called to holiness (CCC 825, 2013). Each person also has a particular vocation: marriage, priesthood, consecrated life, single life lived for God (CCC 914–933, 1877–1879).
God calls through our gifts, circumstances, the Church and conscience. Prayer, the sacraments and spiritual guidance help us hear (CCC 2230–2232).
Parents should foster vocations (CCC 2232). Pray especially for vocations to the priesthood and religious life.
Avoid pressure. Tell students to be open and generous, without anxiety about timing.
quiz: Every Christian is called to…|Fame|Silence|Holiness|Wealth|2|CCC 2013.
Vocation means…|Plan|Call|Job|Hobby|1|Latin vocare.
Discernment involves…|Luck|Coin flips|Prayer and advice|Guessing|2|CCC 2030.
lessons.life: Write a prayer for your vocation.
misc: “God has a secret plan I might miss.”
lessons.mem: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.” (1 Samuel 3:9)
lessons.hook: Read 1 Samuel 3:1–10. Ask: “Why did Samuel not recognize the voice? Who helped him?” Eli. “We too need help to hear.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four vocations and one step toward discerning.

lessons.title: The Law of love
lessons.idea: Jesus gives the New Law, the law of love. It fulfills the Old Law, is written on our hearts by the Spirit, and is summarized in the Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitudes.
lessons.question: What is the New Law?
lessons.activity: “Old Law, New Law” (25 min). Two-column chart comparing Old Law (e.g., “Do not kill”) and the New Law (“Do not even be angry; be reconciled”) using Matthew 5:21–48. Discuss: why is the second harder and more freeing? Add Jesus’ new commandment (John 13:34).
teach: The New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given in Christ, the perfection of the Old (CCC 1965–1966). It is a law of love, grace and freedom (CCC 1972).
The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) is its charter (CCC 1966). Jesus gives a “new commandment”: “Love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34; CCC 1970).
The Law is not abolished but fulfilled (Matthew 5:17). The moral life is a response to love, not only obedience to rules (CCC 1972–1974).
Work with children to apply it to ordinary conflicts.
talk: How is it different from the Old?
quiz: The New Law is…|The Law of love|The Law of fear|A tax|A list of fines|0|CCC 1965.
It is written…|On our hearts by the Spirit|In books only|In stone only|In the sand|0|CCC 1966.
The Old Law…|Is evil|Prepares for the Gospel|Is outdated|Has no value|1|CCC 1963.
lessons.life: Practice one Sermon on the Mount teaching.
misc: “God of the Old Testament was cruel.”
lessons.mem: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you.” (John 13:34)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What’s the difference between a rule and a relationship?” A rule says what to avoid; love asks what more I can give.
lessons.assess: Ask students to compare an Old Law command and Jesus’ deepening of it.

lessons.title: Mortal and venial sin
lessons.idea: Not all sins are equal. Mortal sin destroys love in the heart by a grave violation of God’s law and requires three things: grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent. Venial sin weakens love but does not break our friendship with God.
lessons.question: What makes a sin mortal?
lessons.activity: “Sort and discuss” (25 min). Under teacher guidance, sort anonymous examples into questions: Is the matter grave? Did the person know? Did they freely choose? Discuss why intention and knowledge matter. Close by praying the Act of Contrition and noting God’s mercy.
teach: Mortal sin requires grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). It turns us away from God and needs Confession (CCC 1855–1861).
Venial sin offends but does not kill charity (CCC 1862–1863). Repeated venial sin can lead us toward mortal sin, so we should resist it.
Be careful to address anxiety: those who are worried about their sins are usually not in mortal sin. Encourage trust in God’s mercy (CCC 1864).
Sin has social effects (CCC 1869).
quiz: Mortal sin destroys…|Sleep|Friendship only|Charity in the heart|Nothing|2|CCC 1855.
Which is a condition of mortal sin?|Being tired|Being young|Having money|Full knowledge|3|CCC 1857.
Venial sin…|Is mortal|Is harmless|Wounds but doesn’t destroy charity|Is forgiven automatically|2|CCC 1855.
lessons.life: Learn the Act of Contrition by heart.
lessons.mem: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, and will forgive our sins.” (1 John 1:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is a scratch the same as a broken leg?” Both hurt, but they need different care. Read 1 John 5:16–17.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the three conditions for mortal sin.

lessons.title: Works of mercy
lessons.idea: Works of mercy are loving actions to help people in body and soul. There are seven corporal and seven spiritual. Jesus says we will be judged on how we treated the least of his brothers and sisters.
lessons.question: Which work will you do this month?
lessons.activity: “Mercy project” (30 min). Make a chart of the 14 works with a local example for each. Choose one for a class project (a food drive, visiting the elderly, a prayer chain). Set dates and assign roles.
teach: The corporal works: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned, bury the dead (CCC 2447).
The spiritual works: instruct the ignorant, counsel the doubtful, admonish sinners, comfort the sorrowing, forgive offenses, bear wrongs patiently, pray for the living and the dead (CCC 2447).
“As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). Our love of the poor is a test of faith (CCC 2443–2446).
Add Catholic social teaching in simple form: dignity, family, solidarity, care for creation.
talk: Which work of mercy can you do?
quiz: A corporal work of mercy is…|Feed the hungry|Pray for the dead|Counsel the doubtful|Forgive offenses|0|CCC 2447.
A spiritual work of mercy is…|Instruct the ignorant|Bury the dead|Visit the sick|Clothe the naked|0|CCC 2447.
Jesus says, “Whatever you did for the least…”|You did for me|Was easy|Was fine|You did for them|0|Matthew 25:40.
lessons.life: Do one work of mercy this week.
misc: “Someone else will take care of it.”
lessons.mem: “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 25:31–46 aloud. Ask: “Where was Jesus in the story?” Note the surprise: “I was hungry and you fed me.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three corporal and three spiritual works and give an example each.

lessons.title: The Liturgy of the Hours
lessons.idea: The Liturgy of the Hours is the Church’s daily prayer. Morning Prayer and Evening Prayer are its hinges. It sanctifies the day with psalms, canticles and readings.
lessons.question: What are the hours?
lessons.activity: “Morning Prayer together” (25 min). Pray a short Morning Prayer: opening versicle, hymn, psalm with antiphon, short reading, Benedictus or Magnificat, intercessions, Our Father, blessing. Debrief how the psalms feel.
teach: The Liturgy of the Hours extends the praise of the Eucharist throughout the day (CCC 1174–1178). Priests, religious and many laypeople pray it.
Its core is the Psalms, the prayer of Jesus (CCC 2585–2589). The hours include Office of Readings, Morning, Daytime, Evening and Night Prayer.
Praying the Hours unites us with the whole Church worldwide, who pray in the same rhythm.
Introduce apps or Divine Office books.
quiz: The Liturgy of the Hours is…|A game|A TV show|The Church’s daily prayer|A school subject|2|CCC 1174.
The chief hours are…|None|Noon only|Morning and Evening Prayer|Midnight only|2|CCC 1175.
The main text is…|Letters|The Psalms|Songs|Poems|1|CCC 1177.
lessons.life: Pray a short morning prayer from the Office.
lessons.saint: Benedict: “Prefer nothing to the work of God.”
misc: “The Liturgy of the Hours is only for priests.”
lessons.mem: “Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous ordinances.” (Psalm 119:164)
lessons.hook: Ask, “How often do you check the time? How often do you think of God?” Read Psalm 119:164: “Seven times a day I praise you.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name two hours of prayer and what they contain.

lessons.title: Devotions
lessons.idea: Popular devotions such as the Rosary, the Stations of the Cross, Eucharistic Adoration, novenas and pilgrimages enrich the liturgy and express the faith of ordinary people.
lessons.question: Which devotion do you know?
lessons.activity: “Stations of the Cross” (30 min). Pray the Stations with images, kneeling or standing at each. Afterwards each student chooses a station and writes what it tells them about Jesus’ love. Read Matthew 14:13–21 for another devotion theme (compassion).
teach: Popular piety includes rosaries, pilgrimages, processions, novenas and veneration of relics (CCC 1674–1676). It should be guided by the liturgy and not replace it (CCC 1675).
The Stations of the Cross follow Jesus’ Passion. The Rosary meditates on the life of Christ with Mary. Adoration is quiet prayer before the Blessed Sacrament.
The Church guards against superstition (CCC 2111). Devotions lead to Christ and the sacraments.
Invite families to share devotions from their cultures.
talk: How do they point to Mass?
quiz: Stations of the Cross have…|Seven|Twelve|Ten|Fourteen stations|3|Tradition.
A novena is…|Nine days of prayer|A feast|A meal|A song|0|Acts 1:14.
The Rosary has…|Five mysteries per set|One|Nine|Fifteen|0|Tradition.
lessons.life: Pray the Stations on a Friday in Lent.
lessons.mem: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28)
lessons.hook: Show photos or objects: a rosary, a Station image, a pilgrim’s shell, a novena card. “These are ways Catholics pray outside Mass.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to name two devotions, their purpose and one way to practice.

lessons.title: Prayer in daily life
lessons.idea: We are called to pray at all times, not only at set times. Offer your work, play and troubles to God in a Morning Offering, short prayers during the day, grace before meals, and an evening review.
lessons.question: How can you pray at school?
lessons.activity: “Daily prayer plan” (25 min). Students build a day plan with a morning offering, a mealtime grace, a short prayer for tests or games, and an evening examen. Practice each. Choose one new habit and a reminder to support it. Read 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18.
teach: Paul urges, “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). The Church teaches that prayer is possible always (CCC 2697–2698, 2742–2745).
The Morning Offering gives the day to God. Mealtime grace gives thanks. An evening examen reviews the day (CCC 2658–2660).
Short “aspirations” like the Jesus Prayer keep the heart turned to God (CCC 2666–2668).
Help students handle distraction and dryness with patience (CCC 2729–2733).
talk: How can you pray at school?
quiz: “Pray without ceasing” is from…|Genesis|Mark|Exodus|1 Thessalonians|3|1 Thess 5:17.
A morning offering gives God…|Our day|Our time off|Our homework|Our toys|0|Tradition.
Examen is…|A game|A test|A review of the day with God|A chore|2|Ignatius.
lessons.life: Make a prayer card for school.
lessons.saint: Brother Lawrence: practice of the presence of God.
misc: “I must find a perfect quiet place to pray.”
lessons.mem: “Rejoice always, pray constantly, give thanks in all circumstances.” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What can you do while walking, waiting or washing dishes?” Introduce short prayers: Jesus, I trust in you.
lessons.assess: Ask each student to share their prayer plan for one day.
